utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and in every one in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mrs. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Mundis. And could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President; good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused and everyone else in the courtroom. We have a witness who will be testifying here in a minute, but before we call the witness in, there are certain documents that weren't tendered into evidence yesterday. These documents were used when Mr. Hadzialic was testifying. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We didn't have enough time yesterday to tender the documents into evidence. Out of the five documents shown to Professor Hadzialic, we suggested the following be admitted into evidence. Four documents, document 0977, 0995, 0996, 0981. These are documents recognised by the witness. He commented on the documents, and they relate to the knowledge the witness had in 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to the documents being admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have four numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The references for these documents will be DH977, English version DH977/E. DH981, English version DH981/E. DH995. The English version will be DH995/E. And finally DH996. The English version will be DH996/E. And that completes the list of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Among the documents presented, I have 977, then 995, 996, and 981. The order that you presented these documents in was different, but that doesn't matter, I suppose. I think that Defence counsel wanted to take the floor to make some submissions, but please do so briefly because the witness is waiting. I think it was Mr. Bourgon who had some submissions to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Madam Judge; good day, Your Honour; good day, Mr. President. I would previously like to address the Chamber with regard to the translation issue. We informed the Chamber about a week ago that there would be a meeting between the Registry and the Defence in order to see what we could do to ensure that the documents included in Defence's list might be translated in good time so that they can be used with the witnesses. The Defence is satisfied with the meeting that we had, but nevertheless, we are currently faced with the possibility that a significant number of documents might not be translated in time. The situation up until court recess isn't a problem. However, after the new year, in 2005, the translation issue might and problem. The documents that are required for the hearing of certain witnesses may not have been translated. We are exploring the possibility so that the Registry -- but we would like to inform the Chamber immediately of the problem that might arise. And secondly, Mr. President, there is an another issue I would like to address, but perhaps I'll do so after the witness has been heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the translation issue is concerned, we'll follow this closely. We hope that you will be in a position to ensure that all the documents are translated when the witness is called in January, but there might be a technical possibility. If a document hasn't been entirely translated, you may proceed as you have proceeded to date. You may ask the witness to read out the relevant phrase, the relevant passage in his own language and you can have the document marked for identification and wait for the full translation to be provided at a subsequent date. But in such a case, you should focus on a line, paragraph, or half a page. In such a case, the witness could read out the relevant passage in his own language, and this will be interpreted. This is a technical solution, but there maybe other solutions. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll talk about this with my colleague from the Prosecution. It might be prejudicial to the Prosecution, but if we manage to present the documents to them in advance so that there are no misunderstandings, in such a case this is a possible way of proceeding. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the parties can meet in advance and sort out the problem, it would be preferable to do that than to raise issues before the Trial Chamber, because this takes time which is to the detriment to the proceedings. Naturally you should address us if there are problems you can't deal with, but if you, the Prosecution and the Registry, are in a position to solve the problems that arise and find practical solutions, all we can do is support you in this practical procedure. I will now call the witness into the courtroom. Could the usher please call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I'd first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying into your own language. If so please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names, the date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Brkic Nezir. I was born on the 18th of December, 1942 in Lasva, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphone or speak more loudly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed, and if so, what is your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, were you employed? Did you hold a position of any kind, and if so, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was employed -- I worked for the railways in Zenica, and I worked as the president of the local commune in the Zenica local commune. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the president of the Lasva local commune. Have you already testified about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, either before an international or national court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration that you will be shown in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So before I give the floor to Defence counsel, their examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we will be following today. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel. You know them. You have certainly met them already. They are to your left. Once they have completed their examination-in-chief, which could take up to an hour and a half, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct what we call their cross-examination. As a rule, the Prosecution is granted the same amount of time as the Defence. After this initial stage, if necessary, Defence counsel may put additional questions to you, questions that are related to the Prosecution's questions. Then the three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions either to clarify some of the answers you have provided to the parties or in order to fill in any gaps in your testimony. In such a case, the Judges may show documents and ask you to comment on documents that have already been admitted into evidence. These documents are in the hands of the registrar. If you feel that a question is complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. We don't have any written documents that concern your testimony, so we do not know where you've been. We do not know what you'll be testifying about. This is why your answers are so important, and this is why the comments you make about certain documents that will be shown to you are so important. There are two other factors I would like to draw your attention to, two other important factors. Firstly, you have just taken the solemn declaration, which means that you'll speak the truth and nothing but the truth. This should exclude false testimony, because throughout the world, false testimony is an offence that is sanctioned. A witness could be given a prison sentence or a fine for having given false testimony. But I'm telling you this in order to inform you of the fact. And secondly, this shouldn't be relevant to you, but when a witness answers a question, the information that the witness provides might be used against the witness, but the witness can refuse to answer such a question. However, the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to answer the question, but if this occurs, the witness is granted a form of immunity. This is a measure that exists in order to ensure that the truth is established. You should be aware of the fact that the parties are putting questions to you to establish the truth with regard to the events that you witnessed. You won't be questioned in order to make you feel uneasy. So far, everything has proceeded without any problems, with other witnesses. If there any problems, inform us of the fact. We'll try to deal with them. You should also be aware of the fact that we have to have a break after an hour and a half for technical reasons, and this will allow you to have a brief rest before we resume. Usually we'll have about two 30-minute breaks. And this would allow you to have a rest because by the end of the day you might be very tired. Without wasting any more time on that, I'll give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we briefly go into private session, because I have a request to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, shall we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Brkic. The president of the Trial Chamber has drawn your attention to a number of matters which you should know as a witness before beginning your testimony. I should like to draw your attention to just one further matter. You and I are speaking the same language, and you could easily answer my questions promptly, as soon as you hear them. But please, once you have heard my question, make a pause before beginning your answer so that the interpreters can interpret everything properly so that the Trial Chamber and everybody in the courtroom can follow. Have you understood what I have said?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where are you living now, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I'm currently living in Lasva, where I was born, which is near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I am retired, but I used to work in the railways as a treasurer, a cashier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkic, where is Lasva, in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Lasva is on the border of the Zenica municipality. The local community borders with the municipality of Kakanj and Busovaca. So the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond three meet at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the Lasva consists of several villages, and if so, could you tell us which they are?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Lasva, the local commune of Lasva, consists of four main villages, but then each of those villages has another hamlet. There's Dolipolje across the Bosna River valley downstream from Sarajevo to the right, and to the left is Lasva, Donja Visnjica, Gornja Visnjica, Dusina with its hamlets, Brdo, and Sajtovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, could you tell us who inhabited the Lasva local commune? What was the population -- of which ethnicity was your local commune?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: It was inhabited by Muslims, who are now known as Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs. So all they religions were represented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the majority population there?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: 75 to 80 per cent were Muslims. We didn't have precise figures, but the Serbs and the Croats roughly accounted half each of the rest. We don't really have real statistical data about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you said that the local commune was at an intersection of three municipalities, though you belong to Zenica. Tell me, which villages of your local commune bordered on Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The local commune bordered on Busovaca municipality, and the closest village was Dusina with its hamlets Ducina and Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkic, was the Lasva local commune important for some particular reason for the region and for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I have to go back a little. During the Second World War, Lasva was the main railway junction for Sarajevo, Jajce, and even as far as Drvar. The Germans built through bunkers. One bunker is next to the bridge, then another one across the Visnjica stream, and then a third, because the Germans had a strategic interest in this location. Today, in addition to the railway line going from Sarajevo to Zenica and Doboj, the regional road going to Jajce, Bugojno, Kiseljak passes through Lasva as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the main town that the inhabitants of your local commune would go to most often?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Zenica, because that was where the municipality was. That is where the schools were, secondary schools and university. And the municipality was headquartered there. So all the inhabitants mostly worked in Zenica, either in the ironworks or in the mines, or on the railways. Anyway, mostly Zenica, regardless of ethnicity. Muslim, Croats, and Serbs, all of them worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkic, with the beginning of the war in 1992, did certain changes occur in your local commune, and did a part of the population move away from your local commune?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As I said before, the Lasva local commune was inhabited by all three ethnicities, and shall we say it was one of the best local communes in that sense, in the sense of brotherhood and unity. And we received several tributes. And even just before the war we were rewarded financially because we worked so well together. However, when the referendum took place, that is how it started, for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we and the Croats took part. The Serbs did not want to take part. They organised this plebiscite, and they somehow started withdrawing from certain circles, from cooperation. It was the Serbs who left first because, as far as I know, they were told they had to leave by the new year. They were told to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you find out that the Serb population was going to leave? Did anyone tell you that, or did you read about it somewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I had a good friend who was manager of the post office. Kosta Spiric. He's still alive. He's living in Doboj. We weren't quite house friends, but very good friends. And he told me literally, "Nezir," my nickname was Nesko, "we have to move out from those areas, all of us Serbs. And remember, I will be the last to go, and before leaving, I will come to your house and tell you." He came, and he kissed me. Tears went down his cheeks. He said, "I've kept my promise. We are leaving, but worse things will come, because by the new year this area will have to be inhabited by only one ethnic group." And he was the last to leave, sometime towards the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, after the war started and a mobilisation was called, did the local population respond and join certain military units, that is, the Territorial Defence units as the legitimate army of the country?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to admit it was only the Muslims who responded. But the Serbs were exclusive about it. They said, "We don't want to, and we don't -- we mustn't." And then it turned out that the Croats were self-organising as an HVO unit, and unfortunately not attached to Zenica but to the parish of Busovaca, even though they were inhabitants of the Zenica municipality, and it would have been normal for them to join, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When your population started to organise and form a unit of Territorial Defence, do you know what kind of weapons that village unit had?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I would first like to say something. I was elected president of the local commune, even though I did not long to any party, because of the results I had achieved in the previous period. I was president of the local commune for many years, even though the leading parties were SDA, HDZ, they elected me. I resisted a little. I said, "Why are you electing me?" And they said, "You're a great man of confidential and prestige." That's what they told me. Would you remind me of your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: What weapons those village units of Territorial Defence had.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As there was a military barracks in Zenica, it was common knowledge that the barracks was a threat for the whole municipality and for all of us. And then it was my initiative. I appealed to the people that we organise ourselves and hold guard duty. The Serbs accepted, but they came with sticks. We Muslims had six rifles, but the Croats at that time didn't show any weapons although they had some. Later on it was discovered that they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That brings me to my next question. How did the Croat population organise themselves in your local commune, and when did you find out that they were arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The Croat population, I appealed to them, and not just them, to Serbs as well. I told them about what the old people said, what happened in the Second World War. If an Ustasha came, then a local man would take care that nobody hurt anyone. And the same applied to the Chetniks. A man would be chosen to escort the Chetniks through the village so as not to hurt anyone. The same applied to the Partizans. And then I appealed to them, "Let's avoid all of this." And the Croats sort of accepted, but when I finally discovered what they wanted on the first day of Bajram - I think it was the 4th of April it was a long time ago - Luka Rajic called me and said, "We have to put on a uniform and arm ourselves today." "Who?" I said. And he said, "Our unit?" "What unit? You kept saying that you didn't have any weapons." I asked, "Who gave you such orders?" And he said, "Mr. Kordic." I said, "can I somehow reach this Mr. Kordic?", because I was -- even though I was risking -- I was taking a risk myself. As I live above the railway station, I said I'd wait for you by the railway track. And Luka had his own car. I thought he was alone, but then I saw another two combatants with him. They were wearing uniforms and automatic rifles. I think they were Kalashnikovs. I said, "What's this, boys?" And they said, "We have to put on uniforms." And we reached the brick yards in Busovaca. Somebody said, "Here he is." And it was Kordic. I suppose they recognised his jeep. And we stopped there. And indeed I saw several men. I don't know how many. I didn't pay attention. I didn't count them, but quite a large group. And a truck from which weapons were being distributed. I didn't really want to watch. And Luka called him up, and he came up and he said, "Hello, boys." Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond And then they explained to him what it is I wanted. And he said, "Above Busovaca there's a coffee bar. Go and wait for me there." We waited for about an hour, an hour and a half. He came with an escort. Two guys were with him. He congratulated me on Bajram, and he asked me what it was we wanted. And I said, "Mr. Kordic, you know that we Muslims are celebrating Bajram today, and it's not a good idea for your boys to put on a uniform on this particular day and to go on patrol with weapons. This could -- this would be an unpleasant surprise, and who knows where it could lead." But he said, "But they have to." And I said, "What do you mean?" And he said, "They have to protect you from the Chetniks." And I said, "What Chetniks?" And he enumerated all those villages, and I said not to worry about it. And again I appealed to him not to put on uniforms today, that it was in our common interest. And then he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, after this period, the Bajram holidays, when an HVO unit was formed in Lasva, which brigade of the HVO did it join?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the name of the Busovaca Brigade, but anyway, it was the Busovaca Brigade. And we insisted that they join the Zenica HDZ, or if there's an HVO unit there that they should join the unit over there, because it would be easier for us to work together, but they didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, if I have understood you correctly, you were elected as the president of the local commune by the assembly of the local commune, which was composed of representatives of all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in that capacity in the course of 1992, did you feel that HVO and HDZ representatives were behaving differently, and how did the majority Muslim population react to their behaviour?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Well, it was a grim situation. 70 per cent of those people who first attacked us, let's say the representatives of the local communes. They said, "Why aren't you resisting? Why are you letting them kill us?" But -- that's what they said. But me and my -- I and my associates tried to calm tension, and we tried to contact with the TO staff, the headquarters of Zenica to cool of these problems. But there were provocations, and they started saying, "We'll have a Herceg-Bosna," and they said, "There will be Serbs up to Bosnia." And they said, "We're not interested in the villages Dolipolje and Mahlici [phoen]." It was very provocative. I don't know whether I should start talking about checkpoints, but they started establishing checkpoints. There was a checkpoint at the railway station, and they controlled the neighbours on a daily basis. That was very sad, but we tried to calm our people down. We tried to avoid a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, tell me, in the summer of 1992, why was there more serious conflict between Territorial Defence representatives and HVO units in your local commune? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was this platoon of ours. They formed a TD, a Territorial Defence platoon consisting of 25 men. They had hunting rifles that they used to mount guard. We received a certain number of rifles. There was one light machine-gun among the guns we received. And the Croats, together with the commander, Zvonko, he was their leader, wanted to take five of those 25 weapons we had. We didn't even know how many weapons they had. And then there were certain excesses. So after a few days of negotiations, we came to an agreement. They gave us two members for the Territorial Defence in Lasva. We gave them two rifles, and we had to give them another one. We gave them three rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: How well was the population in your local commune informed about other events in the country, and was there some kind of a relay in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I forgot to mention that. Immediately after that event, the one I've just described, we had a relay above the relay -- above the railway station on a hill, and we worked on this with Sarajevo TV. And since we're in a valley, that relay didn't provide us with a good picture. But there was a second device for a second channel which they misappropriated. No one will admit this. And this device was taken to Pobrijezje, the second device was taken to Pobrijezje above Zenica. So as far as information was concerned, we didn't receive any information from Sarajevo TV. The situation was very difficult for the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to another question, you said that they started establishing checkpoints. Who started setting up checkpoints and where?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a checkpoint from the -- at the junction. It was at the junction, but colleagues of mine will probably tell you more about this. Or a colleague of mine who's a member of the military will tell you more about this, but I can tell you what I know. There was three checkpoints, in Raspotoc [phoen] and then in Nijanici [phoen], and as we insisted on this, we tried to persuade the unit commander of this, we asked for the checkpoint to be moved to the Lasva junction for the protection of the junction. Later on, some guards were placed there, about 20 men at the junction to make sure that no bridges was blown up, because if that happened, the area of Central Bosnia would have come to a bad thing. So in front of the railway station they took a container, and that's where they started controlling our neighbours, our people who passed by on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkic, as far as these misunderstandings among the inhabitants are concerned, did you continue to try and find peaceful solutions to the problems, and did you inform the civilian organs in the Zenica municipality about these matters?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: At the time the Serbs were still living in the area with us, and at some time in May, I think - I can't remember the exact date - we formed a kind of Crisis Staff for the local commune. And there were Serbian and Croat and Muslim representatives there. And every day we held meetings, because there were daily provocations. There was shooting at night from various directions. But we knew who had the greatest number of weapons. Then there were various provocative acts. For example, they would stop some of our neighbours coming back from work. There were always complaints. There were conflicts. Every day we tried to analyse what had happened, and we tried to reach conclusions to prevent this from happening in the future. The Croats all the said that this was fine, but they continued to act as they did. The Serbs, well, they didn't say much, although they had weapons. They just kept silent. And I apologise. Just a minute. Every day we informed the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff and the authorities in Zenica municipality. We informed them of all the new developments in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that HDZ and HVO representatives accepted the conclusions that you adopted at joint meetings. Tell me, did they implement these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1993, did anything happen in the vicinity of your local commune? Were there any events that had a significant effect on relationships within the local commune?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date. I don't know when exactly Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed, but there was an effect on our Croats. They started behaving differently. And whenever there was an incident, a clash, up in Gornji Vakuf or Prozor, this always had an effect on our area. People started organising themselves. People were always excited. They were running to and fro, transporting things in various directions. Whenever something happened in the surroundings this had a get on our area. And especially, this was the time when the events started unfolding in Kiseljak, Busovaca, and Merdani, in Loncari, et cetera. That's about -- well, Merdani was the closest place to Lasva, to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the Lasva junction. It was at a distance of about two or three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, what was happening in Merdani.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: It's true I didn't hear much about that because I was at work every day. But the soldiers who were at the junction and their commander told me that Merdan had been shelled two or three days before the conflict in Lasva or perhaps five or six days before. I don't know exactly. They said that Merdan had been attacked and shelled, that a line had been penetrated. I don't know how they survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, when returning from work, did you notice refugees arriving in Lasva, and if so, where were these refugees arriving from?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, since I couldn't monitor the situation every day, at every meeting at the Crisis Staff, after 1700 hours we would try to examine what had happened. That's how we had organised the Crisis Staff. Every day reports were submitted. There was a Serb who was responsible for reports. There was a Bosniak, and there was a Croat responsible for reports. Refugees were fleeing from Merdan, from Busovaca, from Kacuni, from Slokovici, and they would come to Lasva. Many of them would come to Lasva and stay with, friends, relatives. They were trying to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are Busovaca and Merdan close to the Lasva local commune, and what sort of a distance are we talking?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I said that Merdan was 2 or 3 kilometres away and Busovaca is between 5 and 6 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time in the local commune did you think there was an imminent threat to your local commune, and did you attempt together with HVO representatives to reach some sort of agreement?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As I said, we discussed all these problems every day, and I pleaded with them, especially Zvonko, who was a deputy commander, deputy president in the local commune in a certain sense. He was the driver. He was involved in various affairs, but he didn't want to accept certain things. I told Zvonko: You'll only cause problems for your people and for my people. I -- I begged him. However, it was all to no avail. And just before the conflict, at about 9.00 in the evening, there was no electricity. We called the duty officer in the local commune. He said the Croats were there and they wanted an urgent meeting. We mentioned the people who were there. I asked whether they had weapons, and I said I wouldn't turn up if they didn't -- if they had weapons on them, because I've never carried a weapon. And someone, Kristo Anto came to see me. He said, "Come on, take your weapons outside." Because I went there alone. I was the only Muslim to go there. And there was another Muslim on duty. There was a refugee from Kotor Varos called Siljo. I don't know his real name. And they had weapons again. And I said, "Anto, why did you say that they didn't have any weapons? I can see weapons here." But what was I to do? That's what 21 happened. I asked what the problem was, and they said the troops had arrived at the estuary. I said, "What troops?" He said 100 or 200 of them, I don’t 23 know how many, or what they wanted. Let's drive them away," they said.I said, "Who's going to drive the soldiers away?" "You and I, said Zvonko. I said, “Come on Zvonko, who am I, who are you to do it anyway? They are probably there because they were ordered by someone to turn up. I said, "Zvonko, I’m no expert in these things, I assume that junction has to be guarded." So finally he said, "I'll call a thousand troops from Busovaca." I said, "As far as I'm concerned, Zvonko, you can call as many troops as you want but I'm not going to meddle in those matters as a member of the civilian authorities." I suggested that on the following day at 8.00 they should wait for me at the station and I would turn up. Although I was late for work on that day. I had problems at work. But I justified my absence. I waited for them until half past eight. They didn't turn up. I think it was the 24th or the 25th. I don't know exactly. It was in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You said that you proposed conclusion. What was the nature of that conclusion? What did you suggest?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I suggest we go to the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff in Zenica to reach an agreement down there and for them to say what the task of that army was. And then I said, "Zvonko come back to Zenica." That was also part of the conclusion, that he should return. He accepted that, but he didn't want to go. That's what I assume at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day just before those clashes on the 26th of January, at the meeting of the Crisis Staff and upon returning from work, did you find out that certain HVO members had been arrested? I apologise. Did you find out that the HVO had arrested certain BH army members?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were HVO soldiers who intercepted two of our neighbours. They were neighbours of ours. I don't know where they'd been. I don't know if they had weapons or not, but these two soldiers arrested them and they were taken to some kind of a house. Perhaps Marko Rajic's house. I don't know why this was done. I called Zvonko and I said, "Zvonko don't play around. You started causing problems. Release the men. They're neighbours of yours. You will have to look them in the face tomorrow." I don't know whether he listened to me, but these men were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, where were you on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As I said, every day I went to work in Zenica. I returned at 1600 hours from work. Because I worked in the company as a cashier. If the director or anybody else needed something, I had to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned from -- when did you return from work on that day and what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, some people said, "Have you heard what happened in Lasva?" I said, "No." When I returned home my wife told me certain things. Someone from the local commune called me. Someone's on duty all day and all night. And I was called they said, well, there were Muslims, Croats and Serbs who were on duty. There was someone who was always present there, and I was informed that there was a conflict. There were wounded, dead on both sides. Nothing was official because night was falling. There was nothing official that could be said. However, through the window of the local commune building, I noted a group of Croatian neighbours. I think Ivica Kristo, called Taraba, was leading them. And this other person who was in front of the local commune said there was another group crossing a meadow. There was a Faruk Barucija who was leading them. Where to? Apparently to the school building. I didn't want to get involved in that affair because everyone had their own duties. The army had its own duties, and I was part of the civilian authorities. I did intervene with one commander perhaps. I don't know who that man was. I sent him to see someone. I asked him to make sure that these people weren't maltreated. He said nothing would happen. I said those civilians shouldn't remain in the school for too long and it was too cold. I don't know if they stayed there for long, perhaps two or three hours. I don't know exactly. And later on I found out that the military police had taken those troops away, the troops that had surrendered. They'd taken them to the KP Dom. As far as I heard they took them to the Zenica KP Dom and civilians saw them returned home. Some remained with the Muslims in the neighbourhood. Others went to Zenica by train to stay with family, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, whether on that day or later on -- I'll rephrase that question. I apologise. Awhile ago you said that you heard that there had been men killed on both sides. At the time or later, did you hear anyone had been killed or did you have information of another kind?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I heard that there were men who had been killed on both sides. That's the information I was provided with. But the person who gave me the information was killed. It was an all-out fight. Some troops were advancing from the estuary and they wanted to avoid passing through the village where there were Croats. They wanted to avoid passing through the -- avoid passing through their checkpoints. They Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond wanted to bypass the village and head in the direction of Kacuni. I don't know what sort of a task they had, but the person who told me this is dead. He said that at the first house they reached, the company commander, Camdzic, I think his name was, was killed by a sniper, and the man next to him was killed too. At the time I didn't know who was killing whom. That's what I know. As for a massacre, I never heard anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you know where the wounded or dead were taken to?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As I was working in the railways, as president of the local commune, I had to take certain measures on the basis of instructions from the municipal authorities and the TO staff from Zenica. I formed a unit, CZ, for supplies, and I -- a Civil Defence unit. And I had a good leader who worked very well. And I said there's the Civil Defence in Zenica, and you come to an agreement with them as to what should be done. And they worked very well. They went to clear up the area and took the casualties to Zenica. There was also a lot of cattle roaming around. Whatever they could catch, they gave to Muslim neighbours with a receipt, whether it was a cow or a bull or whatever. So they really worked as professionals. And let me also add, certain Croats would come and take the cattle, but then again, with receipts. Everything had to be registered. Whoever took the cattle and then people who took them back. Everybody had to sign a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you mean CZ, you mean Civil Defence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkic, after this -- the -- this fighting on the 26th of January, did the local commune take any measures to assist the local population that was left behind and to, as far as possible, take care and protect property?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: There's a village above Dusina. It's at a junction of two roads. It's a bit isolated from the other villages. And two or three old ladies were left there. And this guy, the Civil Defence commander, and I told him to go and see those ladies. Somebody could kill them. You never know. Or they could rob them. And what should be done with those ladies and their property? He received instructions from the municipal Civil Defence of Zenica that these ladies should be brought lower down to another village where Bosniaks live, and they were put up with this lady Milka. They spent ten or 15 days there. Whatever food they had and furniture, everything was put there. Then they were also told to collect all the things in those houses and to put them in the school building, so when the Croats returned tomorrow, they could particular up their property. But again, lists were made of all the household goods taken from the houses, and everything was registered. The idea was that it should be returned it their owners one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who collected and listed these items? Was it done by individuals or by a commission?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In the Civil Defence staff in Lasva, there were four men, three Muslims and one Croat, Drago Rajic, who remained living there. And we would send him, as well. Not to load things but simply to be present, to make sure that everything was done well. And I gave strict instructions to make sure that nothing should go missing. You never know. I thought even they might steal something. So a record was kept of everything. And Drago Rajic had no complaints at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this road through Lasva towards Dusina and Kacuni nowadays being used by men, the military, civilians? I mean, at the time did it become a means of communication with free territory?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only route from Zenica to Sarajevo, the one 12 through Lasva, via Kacuni, and then to Fojnica. I don't know exactly how it 13 went from there to Sarajevo. In any case, that was the only communication 14 because the bridge had been destroyed in Visoko, both the railway and the 15 road bridge. The area up there was held by Serbs-Cekrcici. The road on this side, towards Kalinovik, had already been destroyed by Croats, and a road 17 block had been set up. So the only communication went through Lasva. Then 18 around the Heliodrom, from Mostar where people were detained. Two or three 19 months later, people would pass through Lasva to go to their homes. Once at 20 a bus stop I saw a man going from Zavidovici to see relatives in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, since various people and troops were passing through your village, did you take the initiative for civilian municipal authorities to take certain steps so as to be able to fulfil your duties as the civilian authority and to protect the property?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Around the 16th of February, 1993, I wrote a letter, an official letter, though I made several phone calls. I wanted to make sure for myself. And I addressed a letter to the president of Zenica municipality, to the SDA party and the HDZ party, to the chief of MUP, all the important figures that a meeting should be held. And it was held. Whether it was a week later I'm not sure when. And they went to see this settlement Taraba. The Croats went there. They saw what the situation was like. They visited Rajici and Donja Visnjica, and they went to the school, and I asked the gentleman on both sides, "Will you please tell us whether all the property was taken care of properly." Everything was piled up neatly and a piece of paper saying who the owners were. They were full of admiration and they praised all of us, and they said, "If only we had more such people." And then I insisted some Croats were still living there for another month or two, and I insisted on the protection of those Croats and the return of others, that the police should protect those people. And a conclusion was adopted to that effect, and already a day or two later a kind of unit of the police was organised. I don't know exactly what they were called. The police station in Lasva. And in the settlement Kolonija. And no one could pass without them seeing him. And the police did their jobs. I don't know the details. But anyway, they did -- they did say what could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, since in 1993 the conflicts continued between the army and the HVO, the inhabitants in Lasva and the surrounding villages who had left after the 26th of January, did they return or, if not, do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as their return is concerned, I'm not satisfied nor can we be satisfied, but now why? One must be frank. Lasva is an ordinary village. You probably are not familiar with it. And these guys, these Croats who mostly went to Busovaca, Vitez, they went to Croatia, to Canada, to America, they can be found all over. And the village such -- such as Donja Visnjica, their homes their houses are there in Rajici as well. Not a single one has been destroyed. We have a couple that has returned, a couple with their son, without any problems. No one is upsetting them. He has planted strawberries there. He is absolutely comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are now telling me of the situation as it is today, but tell me, did any of your communes -- do any of your communes who are living in Busovaca nearby come to visit their property, their cemeteries, and what are your relationships like? Is there any tension between you or do you exchange normal greetings if they do come to the local commune?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Just below my house there is a Croat who built a house before the war, Batonjic, Mato. I didn't make any difference between ethnicities. I always wanted to protect everything, and I made sure that that house was not touched, and he's very grateful to me for this. And when he comes we have a cup of coffee. We exchange greetings regularly. And not just with him, but there are others too. But there are others who won't even look at me, but I don't care. I don't know what they consider me to be, although I always had the best intentions. These were all younger men than me. I would always address them and treat them as if they were my children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now let me go back once again to 1993. You said that you protected the property, that you took care of it in the school, counting on your neighbours' return. As we see now, many of them have not returned to this day. Tell me, what did the Civil Defence do with those belongings, and on whose instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: A large number of refugees, not just from Busovaca and Merdani and even from Srebrenica, there are three or four families from Srebrenica. There are those from Jajce and Kotor Varos. There are refugees in Lasva. Most of them moved into Serb houses that were empty, and then also into Croat houses. And it was always the Civil Defence who organised this. And the school was about to start working, so these things were in two rooms and the whole corridor. So these things had to be moved out. We didn't know where. And then the commander of the Civil Defence asked the Municipal Staff what to do with those things. And then temporarily those belongings were given to those refugees, but again with a receipt to indicate what -- who took what.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, is there still a record to this day on the way in which these goods were distributed temporarily if they were temporarily given to others to use them instead of being returned to the their owners? The question is, is there a record of all this in your local commune?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the witness's health, I have tried to be as brief as possible in my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It is half past three. Sir, we're going to have a break, which will give you a chance to rest, and we will resume work at 4.00, and the Prosecution will have questions for you. But of course I will also give the floor to the other Defence team who might also have questions for you, and then the Prosecution will cross-examine you. So have a good rest, and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Does the other Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Brkic's testimony does not relate to the charges against Mr. Kubura, and as a result, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon to my colleagues on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brkic, my name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and I'm one of the Prosecutors representing the Prosecution in this case this in afternoon. As the President of the Trial Chamber indicated earlier this afternoon, I am going to ask you a few questions so as to clarify certain things. However, if you feel at any time that you have not understood the question, feel free to interrupt me. I will surely repeat it or rephrase it as you so request. I note your health, and I would take that into consideration. Thank you. Mr. Brkic, apart from your position as president of the local community of Lasva, did you hold any other positions in any other organisations?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was clear enough, but I was the president of the Crisis Staff for a certain period of time. Then Hazim Barucija replaced me, so the two of us took turns. When he joined the army, then I took over again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And were you ever a member of the Lasva Peace Council?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: You mean in the earlier period. Before the war I was the president of the peace council for a long time, but not during this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you just give us an idea of your -- your duties as president of the local community of Lasva. Basically, what does it entail -- or what did it entail?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, the local commune is an institute which improves living conditions in local communes. It takes local actions. It tries to improve living conditions, communications, the water supply system, the electricity system, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And most of all, would I be correct in saying that it assisted in trying to keep peace in the area?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war that wasn't necessary, but in wartime conditions, the local commune Statute didn't provide for that. But we organised ourselves in a certain way on the basis of how we had lived together before the war. We tried to come to an agreement to ensure that the territory wasn't affected, because we thought we should first mount village guards and then Crisis Staffs to analyse the problems on a daily basis and to ensure that these problems did not occur the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of the conflict, was the Lasva school used as the location for negotiations between the Muslims, or the Bosniaks, as referred to, and the Croats so as to maintain peace and stability in the area?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say, because I worked every day. I had certain information. Perhaps my colleague who will be appearing here tomorrow could answer your question. I heard that certain Croatian representatives from Croatia came, and that was at the beginning or in mid-April. I don't know the exact date. It was a long time ago. Something was discussed at the meeting, but as to what was discussed, I don't know as I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But as president of the -- of the local community Lasva, weren't you kept informed and abreast as to what transpired?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I should have been informed, but the situation was such. It was just before the war broke out, and people no longer trusted each other in Bosnia and in -- in the Lasva valley itself. You could see what the Serbs wanted. They didn't want to live with us. I said Croats -- the Croats also started implementing their policies. They started fighting for themselves. They organised themselves in a certain manner. So I found out that there was a meeting, but as to the purpose of the meeting and as to what was discussed at that meeting, I never found out about this, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But -- okay. Let's move then to post -- or, rather, during the outbreak, the actual outbreak of the conflict. Do you know if there was ever an attempt made by the two groups, the two mixed groups, the Muslims and the Croats, to try to negotiate with respect to coming to some peace plan in the area? And that is during the outbreak. Are you aware of any such meeting of the two groups?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I should have been present as the president of the local commune and of the Crisis Staff, but I really don't know anything about this meeting. Where was that meeting held? Could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My -- my information tells me that it was held in the school, the Lasva school.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: During which period?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During the conflict. The very day of the conflict. I think it's 1600 hours in the evening.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that meeting. I know I was in the local commune at 1700 hours with the person on duty, and there were two other member of the Crisis Staff, and we were trying to agree what we should do on the following day. We were trying to organise ourselves. But as for a meeting with two groups, as for a meeting between the army and the HVO, I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, could you, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, tell us if you knew that there was preparation for the attack?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that at least seven to ten days before the attack or the outbreak of the conflict on the 26/1/93 that a large concentration of members of the ABiH was noticeable in the Lasva-Dusina area, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, these troops, as far as I know, because I didn't really meddle in military policies and in their tasks, it wasn't my right, my task was to take care of the civilian population to the extent that was possible at the time. The situation was chaotic, I must say. No one listened to anyone. No one had any respect for anyone, et cetera. I found out that there was some sort of a unit that -- one that consisted of 10, 20, or 50 soldiers, I really wouldn't know, nor do I know what their task was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So then, am I correct in assuming that you personally was never involved in direct preparation for the attack that was to take place on the 26th? You as president of the local commune was not involved in this at all?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that. I wasn't familiar with that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has answered the question, but I'd like to object for the sake of the transcript, because the witness never mentioned an attack, nor did he mention any preparations for an attack, and therefore, there are no grounds upon which my colleague could ask this witness this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if my learned friend would look a couple questions above, I did ask him if there was a presence some seven to ten days before the attack, and he did answer on the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, could you tell us whether you were aware of what transpired on the 26th of January, 1993, in Lasva? Could you tell us if you know what happened? If something happened, could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I haven't intervened, that means that the Prosecution may go ahead and put this question to the witness. The witness may say what happened on the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have already told you what happened. I was at work. I went to work at 6.00 in the morning and returned home at 4.00 p.m. I was told that there were problems in Lasva, that there were men who had been killed and wounded on both sides. I returned home to have lunch with my family. I was called to come to the local commune. I found out that there had been a clash, but that person hadn't been on the site so he couldn't tell me much about it. This happened two or three kilometres above the local commune in a village called Dusina, if there was such a conflict. But I'm not sure of that, nor do I know anything about the nature of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, if I have misunderstood you, but could you tell us the distance between your village and Dusina, as you just said to us, please?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: From my village to Dusina, well, it's -- the distance between the two villages is about a thousand -- 800 to 2.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that something may have transpired on the 26th of January, 1993, but you are not aware of what happened?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question and be perhaps a little more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier on I asked you about the 26th of January, 1993, and a conflict, and you, in response, said to me that the conflict took place in a village a little higher than yours called Dusina. And then you subsequently said that Dusina was about 800 to 2.000 metres away from your village. And my question to you is: Is it your evidence that you were not aware of what may have transpired on the 26th of January in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: My village is between 1.000 and 800 metres and 2.000 metres away from the other village. When I arrived, when I returned from work, I found out -- I was told by certain workers that there had been a -- some kind of clashes in -- in Lasva and that there were men who had been killed and wounded on both sides. I'll repeat this. I returned home. I had lunch. We ate what we had to eat, my family and I. I was called by a person from the local commune who said there was something I had to be informed of. I went to the local commune and asked this person to tell me what the problem was. He said that there had been a clash in Dusina, but he couldn't tell me anything about the number of men who had been killed or the number of men wounded. We tried to see what we could do as civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as the civilian authorities, could you tell us what you did, if you did anything?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I sent a man to see the unit commander in the school where these Croats were kept. This 30-year-old man appeared, and I said, "Please make sure that these people are not maltreated." And he said, "Don't worry. They haven't been maltreated, and they won't be maltreated." That's what he said, literally. I said, "See what you can do." I don't know what the army should have done. And I said, "Make sure that this doesn't last for long because it's very cold." After two or three hours, the problem was solved, because the soldiers were taken by the military police to the Zenica KP Dom. And some of the civilians returned home. Some went back there to families in Zenica, and some remained with their Muslim neighbours in Lasva to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you be able to state for us who was this person that you would have sent to the school? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The man was dead. He died of cancer three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I am not sure if the record has taken -- I'm not sure if we've gotten the record of his name. Could you please give us his name again, please?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Omer Helvida [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you would have sent somebody to the school to investigate, as you stated, and it seems to me, and you could correct me if I'm wrong, that you may have been concerned why you sent somebody to the school. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I am a person who lived with those people very well, and right up until then we were good neighbours, and without any concern, as a person, I asked this man to make sure that there shouldn't be any problems, any trouble there. And I know that what happened to people who were detained in various schools, in various places, and I wanted it make sure that our people did not cause any similar trouble to what the Serbs had done.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What was the prevailing atmosphere on the 26th of January, 1993, in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As I said, I came at 4.00 in the afternoon. This is wintertime. It gets dark by half past four in Bosnia already. And it was dusk. I couldn't see much. But just -- I saw the Croats being brought there as they were going along the road. I saw them through the window. And on the other hand, the man on the duty, Barucija Faruk saying that another part of the population was coming across the fields to the school. That's all I saw because it was already dark by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On that day, in your opinion, what was this conflict all about? Was it a conflict between two armies? Was it?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina went on assignment. I don't know what the assignment was, but they went as some sort of a patrol from the crossroads. And again, this is on the basis of what this associate of mine told me. He worked in the railways too. And then there was all-out fighting, he said. People didn't know who fired at whom. He fled home, in fact. I don't know how to put it otherwise. I'm no specialist. Whether it was an attack or defence or a conflict, anyway, it happened. This company commander was killed from a sniper for no reason, as far as I learnt. He was passing by a house. I know that, too, that they didn't want to go through the villages, not to upset the Croats, not to frighten the Croats. Another man following him who tried to pull him out was also hit, and that is when the all-out shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Trial Chamber's position, could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P649, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't really want to keep you too long, so I'll guide you to the area that I'm looking at, and it's -- it's page 2, really of --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned friend should first lay the foundation for asking this question. We have to know whether the witness is aware at all of this document, whether he ever saw it, and to ask certain questions, and if there are any contradictions and if it's for credibility's sake, then she might ask him questions. But simply to give him a document and ask him to read it, I don't think it is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Henry-Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we went through this on a couple of occasions with my learned friend, and I think I had explained to the Trial Chamber in great detail that, firstly, this is cross-examination, and the length and the breadth of cross-examination is completely different to examination-in-chief. Secondly, once there is some nexus or there is some link with respect to the document, the witness can be asked questions on the document, whether it is to clarify or it's for credibility reasons. This witness is a witness who the Defence brought with respect to the Lasva Valley and what happened in the Lasva Valley. This document speaks entirely to what happened in the Lasva Valley. There's no need under cross-examination for the Prosecution to lay any foundation. Once there's a link, the witness can be asked questions on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me summarise for the Prosecution. This document establishes a link between the -- there is a link between the witness and the document. Indeed, I see that there is mention of the death of HVO members and also of the village of Dusina. So there is a link. As for the document itself, the Defence rightly asks whether the witness is aware of the document. If he knows it, what he says can have some importance. If he's not aware of the document, then clearly his words or his comments about it will have very little value. So Ms. Benjamin, would you ask the witness whether he's familiar with this document, and then ask him about the contents and the link, and then you can ask him about the link between him and the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, if you look at the document, would you be able to say if you're familiar with what's in the document?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I see this document for the first time in my life. I don't know what I could say about it. I -- to be able to comment on it I need to read it. But what you said before, that I was familiar with the Lasva Valley events, Lasva Valley is a considerable area, from the spring of the river to Travnik. So it's a big area. I wish to avoid all confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think the comment referred to the evidence that was led, the area of the Lasva Valley that you were in and Dusina, and it was in that respect that the document was shown to you, or the document is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. Allow me to intervene. The document, P649, that I have in my hands, my impression is that there are two documents. There is the document signed by Dr. Prlic, but there is also another document dated the 26th of January, again by Dr. Prlic. Which document, actually, are you asking him about? Maybe the cause of the misunderstanding. Because the reference to Dusina is in the second document and not in the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the document that's dated 25th of January, 1993. And you're quite right. I think both documents are marked P649, but it is the one that is dated 25th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the document of the 25th of January, go directly to your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And, sir, I would just ask you to look at the second paragraph, and it is a description of -- of what actually took place. And my question to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we're talking of the document dated the 25th of January, according to the indictment, the events in Dusina occurred on the 26th, and I don't know the purpose of these questions by my learned friend about a document and an event that took place prior to that date and are not covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my friend, even in her examination-in-chief, alluded to the fact that Lasva -- the incidents in Lasva took place on the 25th. The incidents in Dusina took place on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said anything like that. The witness spoke about the 25th in the village of Merdani, which is not part of the local commune of Lasva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, the Defence is telling us that regarding the 25th of January, the witness was speaking of the village of Merdani.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness, with all due respect, may have been talking about Merdani, but the witness was in the Lasva area, or his area that he speaks of, on the 25th of January, and I'm sure he is quite competent to guide us through as to what happened. If it is that the Prosecution -- the Defence believes that foundation has to be laid, then I would ask the Trial Chamber to please give us some guidance as to how this would be done in future. And in light of that, I will withdraw the document until we can get further guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can continue with your questions, but in order to save time, go directly to the line with the reference to Dusina and his position as president of the local commune and put the question to him regarding that particular aspect, because let us not forget that he spoke about the Crisis Staff that he set up, and the Crisis Staff was established, apparently, before the 26th. And anyway, I will be asking him about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's precisely why the document was shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But, sir, I'm going to take you, as I said earlier before the interruption, to the second paragraph. I am not sure what page it would be in your language, but I'll take you down to line nine.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please. And line --

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: About people killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can I read it for you in the interests of time? "All Croatian houses in the ethnically mixed village of Dusina have been set alight and the women and children and elderly are subject to downright slaughter and terror." And my question that I wanted to ask to you with respect to that was if you could comment on that for us, if you could shed some light on that report for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you understood the question? There is a document that you're not aware of coming from a Croat entity, and in that document there is the sentence that has been read to you. So the Prosecution is asking what you think about it, what your comment would be regarding that passage. You may have nothing to say. You may say it's false, but what counts is what you're going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just looking at the number of dead, 33. It was nothing like that. I never heard of such a figure. I never heard of any slaughter or lighting of houses as far as I know. But I must say I wasn't on the spot. Maybe I went there a month later to see for myself what had happened to the houses. The houses were quite intact until the next day, when HVO units from Busovaca shelled a house in Kegelji, and the roof tell in. And shells were not dropped only on Dusina but in other villages inhabited by Serbs across the Bosna River. So whoever wrote this, he, in my view, did not have the proper information, although I don't know much about it either. But that so many were killed and that such suffering was caused is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you be able to assist us, if you can, that is, as to which units of the ABiH were present in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I'm unable to discuss those details because I was not involved in the army, nor did I have any right to interfere. They didn't interfere with my civilian activities. So I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But awhile ago you had indicated to us that you had sent one Omer Helvida to the school to see the unit commander in the school where the Croats were kept. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I was quite clear. I came home at 4.00 p.m. I went there at 5 p.m., a call to come by the late Omer who explained to me that there had been problems, that the Croats were being held down there, and I said that I saw some Croats going towards the school. And I appealed to him as a man, as a humanist, and having learnt from the TV and from the press what the Serbs were doing elsewhere to make sure that we didn't act in the same way, that we must save those people and make sure that there's no mistreatment, even though there was no danger to then. He wasn't a commander. He was just some sort of squad leader or something, who was together with five or six men watching that school. And the man told -- told me there hasn't been any mistreatment nor will there be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So am I correct in I'm saying that you cannot assist this Trial Chamber as to, one, which unit or what unit was in the Lasva school on the 26th of January? You cannot assist us here today?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I can't. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I believe, as well, that you will not be able to assist us as to the commander of that unit either?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm just going to ask you just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness said, "Yes, I can't assist you."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We just got it corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you this because you see you were the president of the local community of Lasva, and so I get the impression that you were involved with what was going on and everything that was happening in the community. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: You mean what happened or what should have happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What actually happened in and around the community?
