utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I took all possible steps as far as the civilian authorities are concerned. What happened, happened. One must admit that, that it was my duty as a man, as president of the local commune, to save what could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, I ask you that question because, you see, there's evidence before this Court that certain things transpired, and so I wanted to lay the foundation first. As president of the local community of Lasva, I wanted you -- or, rather, I would like you, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, tell us exactly what your role was and exactly how you were involved to see if you can assist us here.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I've already said this, but I had my tasks to perform as a member of the civilian authorities. At that time, no one could have much control, because people didn't trust each other. There were even Muslims who didn't trust me, because I said, "Listen, let's try to avoid a chaotic situation. Let's try to save what can be saved." And my task was to have meetings of the Crisis Staff, to analyse what had happened, analyse why shooting had broken out. And some Croat, for example, the late Zvonko Rajic, was made responsible to deal with the problems. If there was any shooting among the Muslims, but we didn't have ammunition or anything, because we were guarding every bullet that we had. On the whole we had hunting rifles, but there was a Muslim who had certain responsibilities, and the Serbs didn't shoot. They were preparing to leave, and they left. We analysed what had happened every day. We tried to solve the problems and to ensure that that there were no incidents. That was my main and most important task. I don't know if I have been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think you have tried your best. And let's take, for example, Zvonko Rajic. Would you be aware of what eventually happened to him? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I heard that he was killed. I heard about that. I had to hear about that. I heard that he was killed, and on that day when I returned at 5.00 p.m., I heard that he had been killed, but as to who else had been killed, I don't know. He was a leader. And the first news we obtained concerned Zvonko Rajic. As to how he was killed and who killed him, I don't know. I was working in Zenica. I was 20 kilometres away from that site. The telephones weren't working because there was no electricity. If there's no electricity, the phones lines don't work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But did you come home in the evenings after work? Did you come into the Lasva area where you lived in the evenings after work? Did you come home?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: On that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On that day and prior to that day and after that day. Did you normally come home?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Every day. I went to work and returned, apart from the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So if I were to assess what you have just said and I were to arrive at the conclusion that even though you lived in the Lasva Valley, even though you were president of the local community of the Lasva area, you were not aware of anything that went on? Anything that you knew is what you heard or what somebody told you, am I right?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You had no personal knowledge of any of these things?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What transpired during the conflict on the 25th and on the 26th. Do you know what was the outcome, what was the consequences of the conflict? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: All I knew was what I was told by associates, assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if you feel -- if you don't feel well, tell us. I can see that you don't feel quite comfortable. We can stop if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's no problem. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we just have -- we just have one more question and then I think I'm going to release him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My question to you is: Hasim, Hasim Barucija -- do you know somebody by the name of Hasim Barucija? I'm not sure if I'm correct -- pronouncing it correctly.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: His name is Hasim Barucija, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would he be one of the persons who informed you as to what happened in your absence while the conflict was going on? You referred to people telling you. Would he be one?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. He had his tasks in the army. We wouldn't see each other, or perhaps only once a week to have coffee together, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: reason why I asked the question as to who, you know, might have been informing you as to what transpired.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brkic, my learned colleague asked you whether any meetings were held, as we can see on page 30. I apologise. Let me just have look. On page 35, lines 16 and 17. My colleague asked you whether any meetings were held before the attack or in the course of the attack. My question is -- Mr. Barucija [as interpreted] I apologise. I apologise. There was a translation mistake, but I will ask you this question: As president of the local commune of Lasva, when the troops came to the junction, did you have this meeting that took place before the 26th?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This person, Anto Kristo, came to see me and he said, "Do come." I said, "Anto, I don't want to see any weapons."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We've heard about that. But did you then go to Zenica to see the civilian and military organs and to ask why these troops had appeared at the Lasva junction?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was our conclusion. Then I stayed on after work. I left at 9.00. I even had problems at work because -- and my superior said, "You can't behave like this. If -- you should go home and deal with this."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who didn't come?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Erudzin [phoen] Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague also asked you whether you knew anything about the events that transpired, and you said what you said. You said you had no personal knowledge of the event itself. But tell me, did you see the results of these events? Did you see the people who had been taken to the school? Did you see them being taken to the school? Did you notice the results of what had taken place that day?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I've told you what I saw through the window of the local commune. Ivica Kristo was taking some of the Croatian population away, and Faruk Barucija was leading other people away across a meadow. He was taking these people via another route. The police weren't there. The army wasn't there. They weren't being forced. And there were even old women who had been transported in a car. There were three or four women in a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague showed you P649, the document P649, which I think you still have you -- have before you. It consisted of two documents. One is dated the 25th of January, and the other the 26th of January. Tell me, on the 25th of January in the local commune of Lasva, or in any other village in Lasva, in Dusina, in Kegelj, in Visnjica, was there an armed conflict of any kind or were there any incidents that resulted in death?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the dates, whether it was on the 24th or 25th, with you these two members of the Territorial Defence were arrested. They didn't have weapons. I don't know where they were going. But when I phoned Zvonko and I told him that there was a problem, I said, "Release the people." It looked terrible. That was on the 24th or the 25th. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Had an armed conflict occurred, regardless of whether it was an incident an attack or an action in defence, would you have known or learnt about that event after you returned from Zenica? I'm talking about the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, now whether it was the 25th or on some other day, tell me whether all the Croat houses in the village of Dusina were ever set on fire.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I -- those houses were left intact until the next -- two days later when Croat forces from Busovaca or Kiseljak, I don't know where they were shelling from. Unfortunately they hit the roof of Jozo Kegelj's house, and it burnt down. Those shells were flying towards Lasva, across the Bosna river, because of the hill probably. They were shooting at random, in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, did you ever hear that on that day or the days that followed a slaughter had been committed over women, children, and old men?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: That is out of the question. You have information about what happened, how these things happened. I really don't know because I didn't witness it and don't want to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have just one more question for you. Do you know Hrvoje Sarinic, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Jadranko Prlic? Was he from the area?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I know him from television as prime minister and a minister. I think he's from Herzegovina, from Mostar, somewhere like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, you spoke several times about the late Omer, who told you about the event that took place that day. Can you tell me, if you still remember, what he said to you on that occasion how that conflict started? Let us call it a conflict as well, because you yourself can't define it otherwise. How the conflict started that morning according to what Mr. Omer told you when you came to the local commune building.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: He told me literally. He comes from the village of Dusina, but he was in the Crisis Staff, and he was an honourable man. He had time to tour those places. That day he happened to be in the village of Brdo. What he was doing there, I didn't ask him, nor did I ever learn that. He said, "I noticed that there were troops coming towards Brdo from the junction. They reached the first house." That is what he told me. "Somebody from the Croat houses, there are two or three such houses on a small hill, and somebody shouted, "Halt, I'll shoot." And the boys took shelter behind the house. How many were there he couldn't tell me. And the man going went in front, this Rajic, he said, "What do you want?" And he was hit by a sniper. I suppose those snipers know what they're doing. Then the second guy who was behind him, who wanted to pull him out, he was hit, too, and then the shooting started on all sides. That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. As you were president of the local commune, and all the ethnicities living there, I assume, elected you, which means they had confidence in you, you said that some Croats had stayed behind. They remained to live there for a certain period in your local commune. Did anyone among your Croat neighbours ever give you a different version of the events from the version given to you by Mr. Omer?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As regards Zvonko Rajic and his late father, about seven days later he came to see me at home. He didn't have shoes. He asked me whether I had some shoes to give him. I don't know how come he was left without shoes. And I found some shoes. Even the size was not right, but he said, "That's fine, neighbour." And I said, "Now, what happened?" And he said, "Well, what happened, happened. It's over now."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions, but I would like to appeal to the Trial Chamber that I did not wish to interrupt during the cross-examination as some of the questions related to destruction and looting, which is not part of the indictment, these charges have been withdrawn, and I feel that witnesses should not be questioned about those events now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I? I think I need to respond to my friend, because nowhere in the cross-examination was looting and burning raised. And I think, if I'm not mistaken, the examination-in-chief might have asked questions about houses, and that's how we came to the document and the part that spoke about the Croatian houses. We were talking about the killings. So I just wanted to clarify that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a few questions, because your answers are rather perplexing for me. I shall try to understand what exactly was your function as president of the local community. I would like to know -- the Defence has already asked you about this, but it is important for the Judges to be fully informed. When you were elected, were you elected by the inhabitants of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: According to the statute of the Lasva local commune, which was in force before the war, it was as follows: There was about 1.300 inhabitants, and the Assembly should have consisted of 13 delegates. According to certain percentages that were agreed, there should have been nine Muslims, two Croats, and two Serbs. And all this was abided by fully. The Serbs were those who proposed me as president, the Serbs. I said, don't keep proposing me. I was president for so long before the war. And I was quite tired and exhausted. I was active for 25 years. My purpose was to promote living conditions of my neighbours. Then both Muslims and Croats responded and said, "Zvonko, you have to be president." But I said straight away, "If you're going to be guided by party politics, I won't be the president." And they all agreed, and they said that they would respect me. Then we elected the working bodies, president of the council, of the priest council, various commissions, Civil Defence staffs, and we formed all those bodies at the constituent Assembly. Everything was fine until the referendum was schedule, the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbs were explicit and said, "Don't take it against us, but we're not going to take part, and we have orders not to take part." I -- we and the Croats responded in very large numbers. I was surprised, I must say, that so many people should come to vote which were not interested in the past so much in voting. And everything was fine until the barracks, the military barracks in Zenica, was evacuated. We kept guard duty, village guard duty, together, as I have already said. We had hunting rifles. The Croats had two or three -- I don't know what they really were. Like some special kind of rifle. Drum rifles. And this went on until May. I think it was in May or June that the barracks was evacuated from Zenica, and then the situation deteriorated from one day to the next. That is when we formed the Crisis Staff. Again, four Muslims, two Serbs, two Croats in the Crisis Staff. And I led the Crisis Staff for a month or two, and then I said to myself that it was too tiring because I had to work every day. I have two children and a wife. I had to take care of my family as well. You know, there was a crisis of food. We were hungry. I have to tell you. I'm sorry, but that's how it was. We had to sow and plough in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We understand that you were president of this community for a long time, for at least 25 years.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't always the president. I was sometimes president of the socialist alliance, president of this commission or that, but president of the community for about ten years or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were elected by the 13 delegates, did everyone vote in favour? Were you elected unanimously?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a hundred per cent, a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we deduce from that that you knew virtually all the inhabitants of the village of Dusina, Lasva, Brdo? You must have known everybody.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know each and every one, but most of the population. Didn't know the children, of course. Yes, I enjoyed a great deal of confidence among those people, and I trusted them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that the electoral body -- or, rather, that the electorate had -- or the number of inhabitants was 1.300. Was there a civilian police there for policing work? Who was doing the policing for these 1.300 people? If there's a theft or a traffic accident, who did the policework?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: There was a police station in Lasva. The inhabitants, there were 1.300, but the police station was in Drivusa, nine kilometres away from Lasva, halfway between Lasva and Zenica. Up until -- was it 1991? That is just before the elections in December. There was four or five men who were patrolling every day, but not at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of your elected function, when an inhabitant of the commune died as a result of suicide or due to various accidents, would the president of the commune go to see the person, the conditions of his death? Did this occur in the past 25 years of your activities and mandate?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I am glad to say that we didn't have any such instances. You probably mean murder. That never happened in Lasva, because it was a peaceful oasis. The co-existence was extremely good. I wish to repeat once again. And if somebody should die in a family or should get killed in a car accident or hit by a train or something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But during the 25 years of your active life, surely somebody had an accident. His car turned over or was hurt by an animal. Did that never happen, any such accident?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I hadn't finished my answer. Yes, there were such cases, but then there would be a funeral, and all three faiths would attend, always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when an accident occurs, would the president of the local commune go to see, on the spot, what had happened? Wouldn't he do that to comfort the villagers and to take all the administrative measures required? Did such occasions occur?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Exceptionally. I shall tell you about a case among the Kegelj. A young woman died overnight. It was never established what she was suffering from. And as the local community, we organised going to the funeral together. And then representing Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, we collected money and took a gift to the family. And this was not an isolated occasion. We would do that regardless of the faith of the person involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said a moment ago in answering some questions that within the Crisis Staff you met Mr. Zvonko Rajic. When you learnt of his death, didn't you go to see on the spot the conditions under which he died, even though he was somebody you knew personally? Didn't you feel the need to go and see him, at least to comfort his family and take all the appropriate civil steps? Didn't this -- wasn't this part of your duties as president of the local community?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as going on the spot, I don't know whether you understood me. I was working until 4.00 p.m. that day. I came home, had lunch. I was called to go to the local commune at 5.00 p.m. it was or dark. Now, I if Zvonko Rajic was left on the spot where he died, I assume he was, because the next day all the dead people were collected, both Muslims and Croats, by Civil Defence and taken to the mortuary following the instructions from the Civil Defence of Zenica. The next day, again I went to work. And I said a moment ago that his father came to see me to ask for shoes. I saw him the next day expressed my condolences. His name was Ivo, and I said, "You know, this should never have happened." And he said, "Let that be, neighbour. Let's not take about that now."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must appeal to your memory now. Let's try and go back to the 26th of January. You said that you went to work. Could you tell us exactly at what time you left and how far was your workplace from your home? So when did you leave, and how far was your workplace from your home?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The local train left Kakanj for Zenica at 6.15. This is the workers' train, because the workers in the mines and all the companies -- all workers in Zenica would take this train. I was working in the part -- a department of the railways as an accountant, and I worked until 3.00 p.m., and I took the train at 3.30, and the distance is 18 kilometres by train, the distance between Lasva and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, according to what you are telling us, you got on the train at 6.15, and I heard you mention the Kakanj station. How far is it --

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In Lasva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Lasva station. How far is the Lasva railway station from your home? You must have gone to the station on foot. How far is your house from the station?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Two hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 200 metres away. So if I told you that witnesses have stated that they heard shots, they heard the sound of weapons, they heard the sound of explosions, before 6.00 in the morning -- so given the position you were at at 6.15, didn't you hear anything when you took the train? You heard absolutely nothing? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you where I usually live. I live by the railway sayings, but above me, above my settlement, there's a -- a big hill that protects the village. If there was artillery firing, you wouldn't hear it. And on the hill there's the relay which enabled us to receive TV programmes. So if artillery guns had been firing, I would have probably heard that. But if infantry weapons were used, I couldn't have heard that. The configuration of the land is such that it's difficult to hear these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that when you got on the train at 6.15, everything was peaceful. Nothing happened. There was nothing happening at the time. The village was calm and peaceful. You got on the train to go to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you say that you worked until 1530. While you were at work, no one called you to tell you that something was happening and that it was necessary for you to return as president of the local commune. No one said anything about this.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you went back to your village, and you say that it was only at 1700 hours that you found out that something had happened. At what time exactly did you find out that something had happened?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I've already said I returned home to have lunch with my family. The phone rang. The late Omer Halvida said "Please, come quickly," because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation says you returned to have lunch, but at what time do you ever lunch, 1700 hours? What time do you have lunch.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I returned at 1600 hours, so by the time the food was ready, it was 16.15, 16.30 at the latest. The phone rang. Omer had phoned and said, "Come quickly, I have to tell you something." I said, "Let me just have a bite and I'll turn up." And I went to the local commune and that's where I found out about the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you went to the offices of the local commune. On your way there, on foot, did you see members of the military in the village, any foreigners? Did you see anyone in the village or, as usual, did you only see the villagers or was there no one in the streets, or did you see anything else apart from inhabitants of the village?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, on my way there -- well, the school's above a railway building, but down below I met a neighbour who told me that there was chaos down there and that I should hurry up. But he didn't notice the population moving around a lot. It didn't seem as if there was an emergency until I saw this group of Croats being taken way in a certain direction. But I didn't see any troops until Omer told me that there was some kind of a platoon or detachment, I don't know what, that was providing security for the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kristo, also called Taraba, who is this person? Who is Kristo? Because you say there is a group led by Kristo. Who is Kristo?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: He was a young man, 22 or 23 years old, a big friend of Faruk Barucija. Barucija had a cafe, and Tarabic, Ivica, that's how we called him, as far as I know didn't meddle with the HVO army, but he would see Faruk in that cafe, et cetera. On that day he wasn't in uniform. That's what I found out. Taraba wasn't in uniform. As to who gave them orders and what they were ordered to do. I don't know if they just collected the Croatian inhabitants and took them away, but I know nothing about what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you saw Taraba, he wasn't in uniform and this is a person who would go to Faruk Barucija's cafe. The Kristo -- this person called Kristo, did he have a weapons? Did you see him carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the day when the civilians were being taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he was taking the Croatian civilians away. These were inhabitants of the village whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why didn't you go to see them and ask them what was happening? Why didn't you ask them why there was a group being led by a young man towards a certain location? Didn't you have such intellectual curiosity? Didn't you approach this group that consisted of inhabitants of your village who had elected you?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew what happened to them. Omer told me about them. I felt uneasy about this. It was very unpleasant for me. So I don't know why I didn't approach them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you drew the conclusion that this group of Croatian inhabitants, Croatian villagers who were in certain sense detained, they weren't free, they couldn't move around freely, what was the conclusion that you drew when you saw these people, when you saw these inhabitants of the village, these Croats who were being led it a certain location by Kristo? In your opinion, were they free to come and go, or what conclusion did you draw at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all I was surprised by what was happening. And later, after a certain amount of time had passed, I didn't know. It was a chaotic situation. And during that month, I lost ten kilos because of those problems. I came to the conclusion that in order to avoid incidents and in order to save the population, to shelter them at the time, I concluded that, well, we should wait for it all to be -- we should wait for it all to calm down. But as to who issued this order, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the translation, you said in order to save these people. If you say they should be saved, does that mean that you believed that they were in danger?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, no. Look, it's a village. I don't know how I would answer that question, to be quite frank, but I think they should have been sheltered at that time. The population should have been sheltered until the situation had been dealt with, until the situation had calmed down, if you can understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now half past 5.00. We will have our break, and we will resume at about 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have just a few more questions for you. You said that at 6.15 you got on a train at the Lasva railway station. Is there just one Lasva railway station or a number of railway stations?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Just one railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is this a fairly modern railway station or has it been there for a while?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's an old railway station. It was built at the time of Austro-Hungary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's a very old railway station.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you took the train, did you notice any HVO soldiers at the station? So when you got into the train at 6.15, did you notice any HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I wasn't paying much attention, so I couldn't have seen them. Let me tell you about the train. These were freight wagons, apart for perhaps two wagons which were the usual kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since -- if there had been members of the military at 6.15 at the railway station, especially if there had been 50 of them, you would have noticed them.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Naturally I would have seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to show you a document now. The document is document number P200. This document relates to the Lasva railway station. Could you show me the document. I'd like to check that it's the right one. Have a look at the first page of this document have a look at the last paragraph. It says Zenica there, and in the middle of the paragraph, what can you see in the middle of the paragraph? What can you read in the middle of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: On which page, on the first page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the middle of the paragraph that concerns Zenica. What can you see there?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can read it out. You can read the paragraph out loud.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: "Zenica," is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But not at the beginning of the paragraph, in the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: "There's sporadic shooting from the aggressors." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a paragraph that starts "A group of 50 HVO members"? Is there a paragraph that starts with these words? Can you find them?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: "A group of 50 HVO members which is located in Lasva, the old railway station, the school. The railway station is down by the rails, and the school is up above. And there was someone called Zoran Rajic." I suppose they mean Zvonko. "They opened fire on civilians and BH army members at the Lasva checkpoint. In the morning, the inhabitants of Dusina were attacked by HVO members. They were shelled. They arrested civilians in Dusina and took them away in an unknown direction. In addition to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please speak up.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: "In the morning hours the inhabitants of Dusina were attacked by HVO members and shelled, and on that occasion HVO members arrested civilians from Dusina and took them away in an unknown direction. Apart from the shelling, HVO members opened sniper fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What do you think about what this military document refers to? It's a document from the 3rd Corps. As far as you know, were any civilian arrested by the HVO and taken outside the Dusina village, taken away from the Dusina village? What is stated here -- in your opinion, does what is stated here correspond is to what actually took place, because you returned around 1700 hours. You returned to Lasva. So what you have just read out, would you say that what you read out corresponds to the knowledge you had of the events that had transpired? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say anything about this document, because I didn't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If inhabitants of the village of Dusina had been arrested by the HVO, you would have found out about this in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume I would have found out about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now address the Prosecution, unless my colleagues have questions for the witness. Does the Prosecution have any other questions for the witness? And could we have the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have one question that arises out of the questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, in response to the President of the Trial Chamber, you indicated that when you got home at about 14.30 you received a phone call from Mr. Omer asking you to come right away. My question to you would be: What about your wife, your family. Nobody indicated to you as to what transpired that day, as to how these events unfolded that day? Your family didn't discuss anything about this?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: My wife works in Janjici, an outpatient's clinic about six or seven kilometres from Lasva. She also arrived about half past 2.00 by bus because transportation wasn't regular. There were no buses. She should have come at 12.00, but she arrived at half past two. Then she prepared lunch. The children were still small. She also said something in the case, something's not right, something's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, we're not getting the translation. Could you ask your question again, and I hope the interpretation will come, because I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My question to you, then, was you had indicated to the Trial Chamber that you had gotten home at about 4.30, and then you received a phone call from one Omer who informed -- who asked you to come. A question from the Defence that unfolded. And my question to you is: What happened to your family? You know, nobody indicated to you, you know, what transpired on the day, how the events unfolded? And I think you started to answer. So could you please answer for the benefit of the record, then.

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Can I? As my wife was working and is still working in an outpatient's clinic in Janjici, it is five to seven kilometres from Lasva, she should have arrived about 12.00 or half past twelve, but as the buses were not regular, she arrive at about half past two, and once she got home, she had to prepare lunch for the children and for me. Also, we had a cow in the shed, and she had to take care of all of that. So she didn't have much time to question any developments. She just did say that something appears to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about your neighbours? Nobody was aware of what went on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I was telling you that when I went to the local commune, I met a neighbour, only one, and he said that there are problems, and you better go there, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brkic, I only have two questions for you. One is that you said that you saw through the window of the local commune building a group of people being led by Mr. Kristo Ivica. Tell me, what is the ethnicity of Ivica Kristo, and what was the ethnicity of the people you saw going towards Lasva?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: That's quite clear. Ivica Kristo is a Croat, and these others were all Croats. Yes, that is to make things quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkic, you have answered the question of my learned friend regarding the competencies of the local commune. His Honour asked you to explain your competences in the event of any accidents, deaths, killings, et cetera. Tell me, please, did the local commune before of the war, during the war, and even today ever have the competence to investigate?

utterances.speaker: NEZIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. That's out of the question. The local commune is just a basic cell meant to improve living conditions of the locals, things to do with roads, water supply, electricity supply. And should there be any disputes over boundaries, property, then it might intervene. There was other -- there were other bodies that were responsible for such things, like the police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, sir, your testimony is over. I thank you for coming to The Hague. I know you had to overcome certain problems. We thank you for answering all the questions put to you. We wish you a safe return home, and best wishes for your health. I'm going to ask the usher to be kind enough to escort you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the Defence wanted to take the floor, and as we have some time left, I give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has given me a list for next week. There's one witness for Monday. I'm not going to say the name. Tuesday to be confirmed, Wednesday there's a witness, Thursday there's a witness, and Friday there's a witness. So I'm a little worried about Tuesday. What is the problem? Where do we stand? What are the chances of having someone for Tuesday? So I'm asking the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness for Tuesday is a witness who doesn't appear on our witness list. This is a witness that we haven't met yet, but we have been given a chance to meet this witness on Saturday. To avoid costs for the Tribunal, if the witness can provide information that will be of assistance for the Chamber, then we will call him for Tuesday to avoid him coming -- making two trips to The Hague. I spoke to my colleague about this a moment ago. If we see that this information -- that this witness doesn't have the information that we think he has, then we'll have to make some changes and plan another witness for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. For the moment, everything has not yet been resolved. Would you then call the witness for Wednesday for Tuesday and find someone else for Friday? Otherwise, we'll be losing -- wasting a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, we will fill the week in one way or another. If the witness can't come for Tuesday, we will certainly fill in the time for the whole week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is glad to hear that. We will not be wasting any time, then. As I have already told you, Wednesday, the 7th of December, there won't be any hearing because this courtroom will be used by the Judges for a Plenary. So we won't have a hearing on the 7th of December. Or is it the 8th? No, it's the 8th, Wednesday the 8th. But as the courtroom needs to be prepared for this, the hearing planned for Tuesday will be held, I'm told, in the afternoon, though it should have been in the morning. So at the last moment, Tuesday the 7th, we will have a hearing on -- at 2.15 and not in the morning. I'm sorry. No, I'm sorry. It's the day after, that is the Thursday the 9th when the hearing will be in the afternoon, because they won't -- otherwise, they won't have time to prepare the courtroom. I don't know why, whether they're moving walls or what, but anyway, it will not be possible to sit in the morning on Thursday, but we will be sitting in the afternoon. I wanted to inform you of this. The simplest would be to eliminate the Plenary, but that is impossible. So we won't be having a hearing on Wednesday, the 8th of December. If there are no other matters to deal with, I thank you, and we will meet again for the hearing, which will, as usual, on Friday be in the morning. So tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
